Beállítom Tűz ütött ki vasárnap reggel a Börzsönyben, Szokolya közelében, a Tamás-hegyen – közölte lapunkkal a Börzsönyi Hegyimentő Szolgálat. A lángokat vasárnap reggel vették észre a helyi lakosok. A Katasztrófavédelem és a hegyimentők először drónnal feltérképezték, hogy merre égnek a lángok, majd a hegy oldalában oltottak. Még azelőtt sikerült eloltani a tüzet, hogy elért volna egy közeli fenyvest. „Amennyiben a lángok elérték volna a fenyőerdőt, a tűz terjedése lényegesen gyorsabbá és kiszámíthatatlanabbá válhatott volna, ami sokkal nagyobb területet veszélyeztetett volna” – írta Hegyimentő Szolgálat hozzátéve, hogy így is jelentős területet érintett és komoly károk keletkeztek az erdőben. https://www.thetimes.com/travel/destinat.text: Accessibility Links My quest to find the best bars in Porto — and not just for port Portugal’s second city excels when it comes to cocktails. A lively atmosphere, special hot dogs and great tipples make these six spots particularly irresistible Porto is the gateway to the Douro wine region Getty images Richard Godwin Wednesday September 23 2026, 5.00am BST , The Sunday Times Listen 0:00 / • 7:49 min Share Share this article Email Twitter Facebook Link Save T here is a lot to admire about Porto — one of those attractive, unpretentious, working European cities that’s a pleasure to visit at just about any time of year. It has a handsome river, distinctive architecture (lots of pretty blue and white azulejo tiles), an airport that is only about 15 minutes by taxi from the city centre and a winningly stodgy cuisine that seems to be expressly designed for soaking up its other main attraction, alcohol. As the gateway to the Douro, the oldest officially demarcated wine-growing region in Europe, Porto has an array of excellent wine bars offering everything from vintage port tastings to natural wine flights. Less well heralded is its lively and growing cocktail scene, built on the city’s vernacular drink the porto tonico, a wonderfully refreshing aperitif that really deserves to dethrone the Aperol spritz. Top stories 1 Andrew takes Thames Valley police to court over Jeffrey Epstein investigation Royal family I’ll be honest, this assignment made me nervous. I was concerned not only about the amount of port I was required to ingest but also about spending time with eight bartenders in competitive mode — because, well, bartenders like to drink; hence our evenings off were spent touring the drinking establishments of Porto. Still, I made it home in one piece, with various recipes and addresses scribbled down. The competition was won by the Lithuanian entrant Greta Skamarociute, whose facility with a shaker suggests that Vilnius might be the next go-to cocktailing destination. 1. La Matriarca La Matriarca has a sense of grandeur La Matriarca is named after Beatriz Leitao Carvalhosa Atkinson, the Portuguese matriarch who married Andrew James Symington in 1891 and thus started one of the region’s most venerable wine dynasties. Opened last year by the fifth-generation Symingtons, it occupies a handsome 17th-century townhouse in a classy bit of town and has a nicely lived-in sense of grandeur. There’s a serious Anglo-Portuguese restaurant upstairs serving dishes such as beef Wellington and arroz de cabidela (a kind of bloody risotto) with a stellar wine list. Downstairs is an airy tapas and wine bar in which it’s a pleasure to spend time — a lovely place to start an evening (cocktails from £5; matriarca.pt) . Advertisement 2. Sede Sede serves sophisticated drinks Sede is a classy addition to the Porto bar scene — an elegant, monochrome space inside a handsome, neo-Moorish 1908 building known as the Edificio Arabe. The central bar is as much a social hub as a workstation, and the bartenders create vaguely molecular drinks that are intelligent without becoming homework. I rather liked the Soup of the Day, a sort of gazpacho-gin-and-tonic hybrid that’s much better than it sounds. Three house classics for £17 is seriously good value if you’re used to London prices, and there are decent small plates too — croquetas, kebabs and a clever take on the Filet-O-Fish (dishes from £3; sede-porto.com). 3. Torto Torto wouldn’t feel out of place in Shoreditch There is a grungy quality to Torto on Rua de Jose Falcao, a fun pedestrian stretch of Baixa district. It has won various Portuguese industry awards but doesn’t shout about any of that too loudly. Mostly it’s a bar for people who just really like hanging out in bars: scuzzy punk on the stereo, graffiti on the walls and a cocktail menu that comes in a cassette case. It’s all a little reminiscent of Y2K-era Shoreditch, but the clientele is sexier and the drinks — named after hip-hop classics — are inventive and surprising. I went for a Peanut Macumba, which somehow found room for cognac, chai, pepper, tamarind, grapefruit and peanut. The bartenders were soon on to shots of frozen Fernet-Branca (cocktails from £9; torto-porto.com). Read more Read our full travel guide to Porto 16 of the best hotels in Porto for 2026 21 fun things to do in Porto 4. Atman Speakeasy A short walk from Torto at Praca de Guilherme Gomes Fernandes, Atman is one of those talking-point bars and requires a bit of password rigmarole to get inside, whereupon you are invited to settle on the deep blue sofas and drink in the “experience”. Apparently it’s inspired by the Hindu concept of atman, the fundamental essence that remains when all that is contingent is stripped away — which is weird, because the drinks are the opposite of stripped back. Some hit well — I liked the Optical Illusion, a two-part mezcal creation involving beetroot, pineapple and lapsang tea. But I confess that I groaned when I realised my whisky cocktail came with an unadvertised matcha-style tea ceremony. Maybe stick to the classics? The Catalan bartenders Pau Gonzalez and Daniel Alba can mix a decent martini, and it’s a pleasant spot to catch your breath ( cocktails from £8; @atman.speakeasy on Instagram). 5. Gazela Gazela has a cult following Near the Teatro Nacional Sao Joao on Praca de Batalha, Gazela is more a carbohydrate and melted-cheese delivery system masquerading as a restaurant than a bar. But it is an essential stop on any Porto bar crawl, having acquired a devoted cult following since Anthony Bourdain paid it a visit in his Parts Unknown food-travel show. The draw here is the cachorrinho hot dog: linguica sausage, cheese and chilli butter or oil, toasted within a thin baguette, brushed with melted butter and sliced into crispy mouthfuls (it’s one of the lighter things on the menu). Gazela also serves good cold beer: the Super Bock is what you must order; do not even think of ordering a Sagres — that’s a Lisbon thing (beers from £1, sandwiches from £4; cervejariagazela.pt). 6. Royal Cocktail Club This well-established bar is nicely placed within the central Baixa neighbourhood. Inside it’s dark, intimate and faintly glamorous, with marble, low lighting and a loungey feel. The menu directs you to the elaborate house creations; each entry begins “Legend has it” or “In ancient times”, but don’t let that put you off. The drinks are well balanced and inventive and make excellent use of port. I enjoyed the quetzal, a sort of white-port-based paloma. The head bartender, Daniel Carvalho, makes a legendary negroni too (cocktails from £8; theroyalcocktailclub.pt). Advertisement Where to stay A room at Wine & Books on Rua de Jose Falcao I walked past Wine & Books on the way to Torto and immediately wished that I was staying there. On Rua de Jose Falcao, almost too close to several of the bars above, it occupies a glassy modern building and takes its theme from two of the great Portuguese cultural exports: wine and literature. It’s also a couple of minutes’ walk from the extraordinary Livraria Lello, the city’s famed neogothic bookshop, so you can spend the afternoon browsing the shelves before settling in for a drink on the hotel’s rooftop for a glass of Douro. The rooms are comfortable and contemporary without overdoing the theme, and there’s a small spa for steaming away any sins (B&B doubles from £165; winebookshotels.com).
